destination.title: Their Son Was Charged. The City Came for His Parents' House.

short28: A court ordered a family's home seized — not because they broke the law, but because their house supposedly did.
Christos Sourovelis painted houses and earned a modest home in northeast Philadelphia.
In March 2014, his twenty-two-year-old son sold about forty dollars of heroin to a police informant.
So the city moved — not against the son, but against the house.
Using civil forfeiture, prosecutors won an order to seize and seal the home with no family member present.
The property itself becomes the defendant — the State versus one house — and innocent owners must prove their own home did nothing wrong.

From 2002 to 2014, Philadelphia forfeiture took more than twelve hundred homes and over fifty million dollars in cash — the typical seizure just a hundred seventy-eight dollars — with millions a year flowing into police and prosecutor budgets.
The family and the Institute for Justice filed a class action, and in 2018 the city agreed to dismantle the machine.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: But in 2014, none of that had happened yet.
And the family who owned it had never been charged with anything at all.
In March of 2014, their twenty-two-year-old son, Yianni, made a decision that would reach far past himself.
On the eighth of May, prosecutors walked into a courtroom with no one from the family present, and walked out with an order to **seize and seal** the Sourovelis home.

Read a civil-forfeiture docket and you will find the state suing an *object* — because an object cannot afford a lawyer, and an object can never say, "but I did nothing wrong." So the Sourovelises did the only thing they could.
It was called **Courtroom 478**, on an upper floor of Philadelphia's City Hall.
And if you missed a date — if you couldn't get off work, if the letter never reached you, if you didn't understand — you could lose your home automatically, by default.
Between 2002 and 2014, the city of Philadelphia used civil forfeiture to take more than **twelve hundred homes**.
This machine was never built to bring down drug lords.
And in 2018, Philadelphia gave up the machine itself.
No more taking small amounts of cash from people who were never even arrested.
The city also created a **three-million-dollar fund** to pay back the people it had taken from — with those never convicted of anything able to recover the full value of what they'd lost.
And Courtroom 478 — the room with no judge — was closed for good.
Christos Sourovelis never set out to change the law.

lines.text: In Philadelphia, if you wanted to fight for your own house, you went to a room upstairs in City Hall. Courtroom 478. There was no judge in it.
source_lines: It was called **Courtroom 478**, on an upper floor of Philadelphia's City Hall.
But calling it a courtroom is generous. There was no judge in Courtroom 478.

lines.text: The hearings were run by the same prosecutors trying to take your property. No court appointed lawyers. No right to counsel at all.
source_lines: The proceedings were run by the very prosecutors trying to take your property. There were no court-appointed lawyers — no right to counsel at all.

lines.text: Owners were handed forms and quietly encouraged not to fight. Miss a date, because work would not let you off or the letter never reached you, and you could lose your home by default.
source_lines: Owners were handed forms and, more often than not, encouraged simply not to fight.
And if you missed a date — if you couldn't get off work, if the letter never reached you, if you didn't understand — you could lose your home automatically, by default.

lines.text: This was not a place where justice was weighed. It was a collection department with the seal of the state on the door.
source_lines: This was not a place where justice was weighed. It was a collection department with the seal of the state on the door.

lines.text: In an ordinary criminal case the government must prove a person's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
source_lines: In an ordinary criminal case, the government accuses a *person*, and it has to prove that person's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

lines.text: In that room the promise ran backwards. They took first, and left you to prove your way home.
source_lines: In Philadelphia, for years, that promise ran backwards. They took first, and left you to prove your way home.

lines.text: It was built to take small amounts from the people least able to fight City Hall.
source_lines: It was built to take small amounts, from ordinary people — the people with the least ability to hire a lawyer, take a day off work, and fight City Hall.

lines.text: Courtroom 478 was closed for good in 2018. Between 2002 and 2014 the city had already taken more than twelve hundred homes.
source_lines: And Courtroom 478 — the room with no judge — was closed for good.
Between 2002 and 2014, the city of Philadelphia used civil forfeiture to take more than **twelve hundred homes**.

shorts.avoids: Short 28 ran the seizure order and the citywide totals; this cut never leaves Courtroom 478, the room-level procedure that made losing a home automatic.

shorts.angle: To get back into the home the city had sealed, the parents had to sign an agreement barring their own son from it.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: What they did after they got the house back, when they could simply have walked away.
shorts.loop_join: L5 ends on the knock still coming for other people, and L1 opens on that exact knock at the door.

lines.text: There was no warning and no hearing. Just a knock at the door, and an instruction: pack a bag, and get out. The family had been charged with nothing.
source_lines: There was no warning. There was no hearing. There was a knock at the door, and an instruction that sounds impossible for a home someone actually owns: pack a bag, and get out.
And the family who owned it had never been charged with anything at all.

lines.text: For about a week they slept on a relative's couch, made homeless in their own city, while the government held the deed to their home.
source_lines: For about a week, they slept on a relative's couch — a family made homeless in their own city, while the government held the deed to their home like a hostage.

lines.text: Then the city let them back in, on one condition. The father had to sign an agreement barring his own son from the house.
source_lines: They were finally allowed back inside on a single condition. Christos had to sign an agreement promising to bar his own son from the house.

lines.text: To get their home back, these parents had to give up their son at the door. It could just as easily have been your address, not because you did anything, but because someone under your roof did.
source_lines: Read that again. To get their home back, these parents had to give up their son at the door.
It could just as easily have been yours — not because you did anything, but because someone under your roof did, or because an officer decided the cash in your pocket looked suspicious.

lines.text: He painted houses. He and his wife earned that home one wall at a time.
source_lines: Christos Sourovelis painted houses for a living.
He and his wife, Markela, had earned it one wall at a time.

lines.text: What happened to them was not built for criminals. It was built for people exactly like them.
source_lines: what happened to the Sourovelises was not built for criminals. It was built for people exactly like them.

lines.text: The city that sealed his door was the city he paid his taxes to.
source_lines: The door Christos had paid for, in the neighborhood he'd chosen to grow old in, was sealed shut by the same city he paid his taxes to.

lines.text: They kept the house. They did not drop the class action for everyone still facing that knock.
source_lines: The Sourovelises got their own home free within about a year — the city quietly dropped its case against their house, and they kept it.
They didn't drop the class action.
